newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook-fundamentals eyed for next move.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook-fundamentals eyed for next move.

text.p: Fundamentals in the U.S. cash crude market look to be key for price direction the remainder of the week, despite a technical selloff which sliced the better part of a dollar off July NYMEX crude oil prices on Tuesday, traders and analysts said.
A very long position in the futures market, as seen in the recent Committment of Traders report, triggered a sell-off by funds on Tuesday.
July crude prices recovered somewhat on Wednesday, consolidating losses to move around 5 cents higher to $20.85-$20.95 a barrel in late morning trade.
The market's focus has turned to the American Petroleum Institute (API) report to be released later today, and whether fundamentals can offer incentive to alter prices.

"These fundamentals are a bit on the bearish side, with the way crude has been building. In general, gasoline season has been a disappointment so far," said Tom Bentz, head of energy trading at High Yield Analytics in New York.

Last week's API inventory data showed crude stocks down some 5.94 million barrels, but the year-on-year data remained bearish with current crude stocks 20.62 million barrels greater than in same period 1996.

Domestic cash traders expected grade differentials to troll near current ranges, until a clearer picture on the Brent-WTI arbitrage emerges and refiners re-enter bidding following the long weekend and the end to June business.
Foreign imports to the U.S. Gulf were quiet, but buyers saw plenty of barrels around, notably sweet foreigns like North Sea Brent and Nigerian grades despite narrower arb spreads.
"There seem to be plenty of barrels on offer of the kind we like to buy, but the arb is going to change some things," said a cash dealer.
Brent was on offer into the Gulf at July West Texas Intermediate/Cushing -65 cents for first-half July delivery.

Sour crudes were expected to benefit from Iraq cutting two Basrah Light cargoes for 2.2 million barrels, on worries the proceeds from the sales would overshoot the oil-for-food deal's $2.14 billion sales limit.
Positioning ahead of next week's review for renewing the Iraq oil accord was also expected later this week.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan was seen submitting his recommendations to the U.N. Security Council early next week, with council action to follow ahead of the deal's expiration June 7.
--New York Energy Desk, Patrick Connole, Patricia Garip-Bertuol ((+1 212 859 1620))
